extracted.intended_audience: program managers, analysts, and decisionmakers evaluating in-house vs. contracted computer/MIS services (Navy/DoD context)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate whether a government-managed MIS (HRMIN) should remain in-house or be contracted out, using OMB Circular A-76 cost-comparison methodology, benchmarking, and site-selection criteria. Includes technical, security, management-control, maintenance, and cost factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: System Performance and Reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: System performance: how well the system supports and performs the function of the application running on it. System reliability: the ability of a system to provide dependable support on a continuous basis (90% up-time and a back-up system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a primary evaluation criterion for alternative locations; performance is function-specific and reliability is operational continuity (explicit 90% uptime and backup requirement given).

rubrics_metrics.name: System and Data Security
rubrics_metrics.description: Security was defined as providing an acceptable level of protection against unauthorized access to the system and to HRM Survey data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider protection of programs and data, access procedures, and vendor safeguards when evaluating timesharing or remote solutions; security issues are accentuated in timesharing environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management Control
rubrics_metrics.description: The ease with which the sponsor can monitor the performance of the system and, if necessary, re-direct the management or content of the application so that the plans or objectives for the system are effectively used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessability and sponsor oversight are key—evaluate the alternative's capacity to allow sponsor monitoring and to effect timely changes to management or application content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance and Operational Support
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of the managing organization at the location to provide adequate personnel resources for the maintenance and operation of the system hardware and software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include availability of qualified staff, local support infrastructure, and anticipated personnel requirements for full operation (examples of realistic personnel requirements are provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost was the final criterion used to evaluate the alternative locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although listed last by the Booz‑Allen study, cost is decisive in practice; note the study's convention that a 'high' rating for this category means lower costs (i.e., cost‑beneficial). Cost comparisons should follow OMB A‑76 methodology and include all pertinent costs affected by the selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of Economic Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic analyses are used either to assess the economic consequences of a decision already made, or as part of the decisionmaking process to compare alternatives as input to decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether the cost-comparison is retrospective (assessment) or prospective (selection aid), as this affects framing and interpretation of results (see Figure 5 flow).

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-76 policy precepts and requirement for cost comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Three precepts: (1) The Government's business is not to be in business; (2) certain functions are inherently governmental and therefore mandate performance by federal employees; (3) the American people are entitled to economy in Government. If a function is not inherently governmental and a public-sector organization is capable, a cost comparison must be conducted to identify the least costly method to the taxpayer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any decision whether to contract out must be grounded in these policy precepts and implement the A‑76 procedures/flowchart; if work is not inherently governmental, conduct a formal A‑76 cost comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmarking (vendor evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A benchmark is a mix of requirements representative of the user's projected workload; mandatory and desired specifications are presented to bidders (e.g., data storage and software requirements). Vendors run benchmark jobs and are graded using a scheme devised by the proposer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use representative benchmark workloads in RFPs to elicit realistic proposals; include test programs and mandatory/spec lists. Note: competitive bidding and negotiation skills can greatly affect contract prices—this is a limitation of benchmarking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timesharing cost elements (typical charges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vendors base charges on some or a combination of: connect time (active transmission duration), CPU time (period a program occupies CPU), storage capacity, channel time (I/O requests), and additional charges (file access, languages, applications, terminal/comm equipment rentals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these components explicitly when modeling timesharing alternatives; use authorized schedule prices (e.g., TSP) for connect time and adjust vendor charges accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timesharing benefits (evaluative dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential benefits of contracting computer services include: fewer programming errors; no training required; known costs; no equipment maintenance (and other logistic support); minimum personnel problems; increased experience and capability for future expanded efforts; greater capability for handling varying workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account qualitatively or quantitatively for these benefits when comparing to in-house operation; benefits are often intangible and hard to quantify but relevant to selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timesharing disadvantages (evaluative risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical disadvantages include: can be needlessly expensive for users who don't need quick responses or have high transaction volume; introduces overhead that users ultimately pay for; usage delays due to lines or system issues; accentuated data security problems requiring safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh these disadvantages against benefits; pay particular attention to security, turnaround-time needs, communication costs, and vendor overhead markup.

rubrics_metrics.name: MIS value via time compression (Krauss benefits list)
rubrics_metrics.description: MIS value centers on time saved: render faster decisions (detect opportunities, identify problems, define/analyze situations, evaluate alternatives); accomplish more in available time (think more deeply, ponder variables, gauge ramifications); make a more thorough analysis (review more information, use advanced techniques, simulate conditions, ask 'what if' questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing MIS alternatives, evaluate how each alternative compresses the management-control cycle and increases perceived managerial value through improved decision speed and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-time management control objective (management-control cycle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A key objective is to minimize time between detection of out-of-control condition and execution of corrective action. The management-control cycle stages include measurement, detection, communication, situation analysis, decisionmaking, notification/setup, and execution of corrective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a system (especially real-time computer-based systems) compresses these time intervals; shorter react-and-rectify time often yields substantial economies and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit assessment model (P x R x U)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three benefit factors: Potential Contribution (P) — value attached to information based on predetermined specifications; Received Value (R) — portion of potential contribution normally received by users; Utilization Value (U) — portion of received value users can apply in performing functions. Realized Value = P x R x U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this multiplicative model to measure perceived effectiveness or 'realized value' of information systems; remember it measures perceived rather than demonstrated effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-comparison scope and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost comparison will account for all pertinent costs affected by alternative selection; costs related to management and operation at program-manager and user sites will not be considered. Assumptions: no differences in cost acceleration between alternatives, inflation/differentials remain constant, and current system requirements will not change over system life (analysis presented for base year FY1982 only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state included/excluded costs and critical assumptions upfront; recognize the limitations (e.g., assuming constant requirements may be unreasonable) and adjust or qualify conclusions accordingly.
